place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the long dormitory bed

setup.zh: 腊月初八的夜。钱掌柜在老槐树底下收摊，给阿禾数出一百文。夜里，孙二狗摸到你铺前。
setup.en: The night of the eighth of the twelfth month. Money-Keeper Qian, packing up under the pagoda tree, counts a hundred cash out to A He. At night Sun Ergou creeps to your bunk.

recap.zh: 大比那夜，钱掌柜一文不少赔了阿禾一百文；孙二狗说：「是你拉的。」你给家里写了第一封信：「娘，漏勺也能打水。」木牌轻轻烫了一下——那张饼，还欠着。
recap.en: The night of the contest Money-Keeper Qian paid A He her hundred cash to the coin; Sun Ergou said, "You pulled me." You wrote your first letter home: "Ma, a skimmer can carry water too." The token warmed, just a little — the flatbread is still owed.

en: "Ma, a skimmer can carry water too."

story.zh:
天黑下来的时候，钱掌柜在老槐树底下收摊，看见阿禾过来，从怀里摸出一个小纸包，放在秤盘上称了一称，递给她：「周姑娘。一文，一赔一百——你押的时候，板上写的是一赔一百。后来我要往上改，没改成，那是后来的事，跟你不相干。一百文，你数一数。」阿禾打开纸包，一文一文地数，数到一百，一文不多，一文不少。收摊的一个老弟子咂了咂嘴：「钱半文，钱半文。多一文不要，差半文不卖——这名号，倒不是白叫的。」钱掌柜把秤杆往肩上一扛，走了几步，回过头来冲小满道：「沈小满。明年还押你。」

小满道：「……他不是从来不认账的么？」阿禾道：「人人都这么说，可人人都没押中过。没押中过的人说他不认账，这话能信么？押中的人才知道。押中的人，又都不说。」她翻开小本子，记了一行，小满瞥见了：**腊月初八。押沈小满，一文。赢一百文。利息：不收。**「不收」两个字，写得比别的字都小。那一文钱，是她进山门时她娘缝在她衣角里的——出门在外，身上不能一个子儿都没有，有一个，就不算穷。腊月初八那天早上，她弃了权，拿剪子挑开了线，把它押在了一个谁也不押的人身上。她合上本子，只说了两个字：「藏好。」

那一夜女弟子那边的油灯，又亮到了后半夜。小本子上，这一页只有三行：

> 腊月初八。一百文，寄家，给弟弟。
>
> 他的，不收。
>
> 他今天没藏。

那天夜里，人都睡下了以后，孙二狗摸到了小满的铺位跟前，蹲了好一会儿，才小声道：「沈师兄。第一轮……你是故意输给我的吧？」小满道：「不是。我脚滑。」孙二狗道：「五行台上的石头，是干的。」小满道：「我脚汗多。」孙二狗便不说话了。他从腰里解下那个蓝布包，断了的那根绳子，他已经拿线接上了，接得歪歪扭扭。他道：「沈师兄，我今天……倒了七回。我娘说，人倒了不丢人，倒了不起来才丢人。」他咧嘴笑了一下，扯着下巴上的伤，嘶了一口气，「台上倒了七回，起来了七回。下了台，在石阶上坐下去那一回……我是真起不来了。是你拉的。」小满没有说话。黑暗里，他听见孙二狗摸回了自己的铺位，躺下去的时候，还小声地念叨了一句：「……记着了。」隔了一会儿，黑地里又传来他的声音：「沈师兄，你会写字吧？」小满道：「会几个。」孙二狗道：「明天……你替我写一封信。我娘不识字，村里有个先生会念。你就写：娘，我赢了一场。」他顿了一顿，「别写是怎么赢的。」
story.en:
At nightfall Money-Keeper Qian was packing up under the pagoda tree. Seeing A He come, he took a small paper packet from his coat, weighed it on the scale and handed it to her: "Miss Zhou. One cash, one to a hundred — when you bet, the board said one to a hundred. Later I meant to raise it and didn't; that's later, nothing to do with you. A hundred cash — count it." She opened it and counted coin by coin to a hundred, not one more, not one less. A senior packing up nearby smacked his lips: "Qian Half-Cash, Qian Half-Cash. Won't take a cash over, won't sell a half-cash under — he's earned the name." Qian shouldered his steelyard, walked a few steps, and looked back at Xiaoman: "Shen Xiaoman. I'll bet on you next year."

"…Didn't they say he never pays?" "Everyone says so, and nobody's ever won. People who never won say he doesn't pay — can you believe that? Only the winners know. And the winners don't talk." She opened her notebook and wrote a line; Xiaoman glimpsed it: **Eighth of the twelfth month. Bet on Shen Xiaoman, one cash. Won a hundred. Interest: none charged.** The words none charged were written smaller than the rest. That one cash her mother had sewn into her hem when she entered the gate — away from home you mustn't be without a single coin; with one, you're not poor. On the morning of the eighth she'd withdrawn, snipped the thread with scissors, and bet it on the one boy nobody bet on. She closed the notebook and said just two words: "Hide well."

That night the oil lamp on the girls' side burned again till past midnight. On this page of the notebook there were only three lines:

> Eighth of the twelfth month. A hundred cash, sent home, for my brother.
>
> His: no charge.
>
> Today he didn't hide.

That night, when everyone was asleep, Sun Ergou crept to Xiaoman's bunk and crouched a long while before he whispered: "Brother Shen. The first round… you lost on purpose, didn't you?" "No. My foot slipped." "The stones on the platform are dry." "My feet sweat." Sun Ergou said no more. He untied the blue pouch; the snapped string he'd already mended with thread, crooked. "Brother Shen, today I… fell seven times. Ma says falling down's no shame; not getting up is." He grinned, pulled at the cut on his chin, and hissed. "Seven times down on the stage, seven times up. Off the stage, when I sat on the steps… I really couldn't get up. You pulled me." Xiaoman said nothing. In the dark he heard Sun Ergou feel his way back to his bunk, and as he lay down he murmured: "…I'll remember." After a while his voice came again out of the dark: "Brother Shen, you can write, can't you?" "A few words." "Tomorrow… write a letter for me. My ma can't read; there's a teacher in the village who'll read it to her. Just write: Ma, I won a bout." A pause. "Don't write how."

exits.means: rests, ends the day, or asks what comes next

story.zh:
话分两头。沉鼎观的大比有一颗丹；同是腊月初八，千里以西，雍州太华山上，也有一个十三岁的孩子，这一夜要吃下一颗丹。那里是太一宫，这一天，做年终大典。

殿前那座台子，又加了一层。石头是从山下一块一块背上来的，今年加的这一层还没干透，台阶上结着白霜。九个真传穿着白衣，排在台下，最末一个是赵昂。他十三岁，跟蒙山沈家那个孩子生在同一个腊月里，个子在九个人里最矮，站得却最直。他仰着头看那座台，心想：等它通了天，我站在上头。

东溟坐在殿上，一动也不动。他从来不站起来，也从来不伸手：递东西的是执事，传话的是执事，罚人的也是执事。每回开口之前，他都要抬起眼皮，往殿顶那一方天窗看一眼，像是在看天上有没有人在看他。赵昂一直当那是师父不屑于动手。这一回，东溟往天窗看了一眼，开口了，声音不高，满殿都听得清：「昂，上来。」

赵昂走上殿去，跪下。东溟道：「吾儿。」

满殿的人都愣了。九个真传，他从来只叫名字。赵昂跪在那里，身子晃了一晃，眼眶一热。东溟又道：「明年秋，你去冀州。那边的水底下，有一样东西，该归太一宫。」一个执事上前一步，替他问那句规矩里的话：「真传赵昂，可有二心？」

赵昂没有答。他从背上解下那口剑——师兄「下山了」以后，执事交给他的那一口——拧开剑鞘的底，从夹层里抽出一张叠成指甲大的纸条。那是他前些日子才摸到的，师兄的字：**昂弟：台上冷，别上去。**他看了一眼，走到殿角的火盆跟前，当着东溟的面，扔了进去。纸条在火里卷了一卷，没了。他回过身来，跪下：「没有。」东溟没有动，只又往天窗看了一眼。

那天夜里，一个执事端着一只玉碟进了他的屋子，碟里一颗丹，不说是什么丹，捏开他的嘴放了进去。他在榻上疼了一夜，天亮的时候，筑了基。十三岁。他坐起来，头一件事，是摸了摸剑鞘的夹层。空的。那是他这辈子，唯一一封写给他的信。

小满趴在铺上，就着窗外的月光，给家里写了第一封信。他头一句写的是「娘，我当上仙人了」，擦了；第二句写「娘，我打赢了马小宝」，想了想，这话要是传到村里，马三怕是要上门，又擦了。末了只写成了这么几行：

**娘：我进仙门了。一年五两，观里说腊月就送到家。屋顶修一修。盆可以收起来了，十七个都收。给我爹买一副护膝，狗皮的。给吴婆婆，再送一条鹿腿，这回是买的。我在这里很好。有人欺负我，我记着账。有几笔，已经还上了。——小满**

他把信折好，想了想，又打开来，在最底下添了一行：**娘，漏勺也能打水。**信压在枕头底下，明天一早交给周衡，跟沈家那一包五两银子一车送下山。他握着胸口的木牌，小声道：「你欠我的那张饼……还欠着吧？」木牌轻轻地，烫了一下。像是在说：**还欠着。**
story.en:
Meanwhile — Chending's contest had one pill; and on that same eighth of the twelfth month, a thousand li to the west, on Mount Taihua in Yong, there was a thirteen-year-old too who would swallow a pill that night. That was the Palace of the Supreme One, and that day it held its year-end rite.

The platform before the hall had gone up another layer. The stones were carried up from the foot of the mountain one by one; this year's layer wasn't dry yet, and frost lay on its steps. Nine chosen disciples in white stood in a row below it, and the last was Zhao Ang. He was thirteen, born in the same twelfth month as the Shen boy of Meng Mountain; shortest of the nine, and standing straightest. He looked up at the platform and thought: when it reaches heaven, I'll stand on top.

Dongming sat in the hall and did not move. He never stood, and he never reached out a hand: stewards passed things, stewards carried words, stewards did the punishing. Before he spoke he always raised his eyes to the skylight in the roof, as if to see whether anyone up there was watching him. Zhao Ang had always taken it that the master disdained to lift a hand. This time Dongming glanced at the skylight and spoke, not loudly; the whole hall heard: "Ang. Come up."

Zhao Ang went up into the hall and knelt. Dongming said: "My son."

The whole hall froze. Nine chosen disciples, and he only ever called them by name. Zhao Ang, kneeling, swayed, and his eyes went hot. Dongming went on: "Next autumn, you go to Ji. Under the water there is a thing that belongs to the Supreme One." A steward stepped forward and asked the question the rules required, for him: "Chosen disciple Zhao Ang — have you a second heart?"

Zhao Ang didn't answer. He unslung the sword from his back — the one the stewards gave him after his senior brother "went down the mountain" — unscrewed the end of the scabbard, and drew from its hollow a slip of paper folded to the size of a fingernail. He had found it only days before, in his senior brother's hand: **Brother Ang: it's cold up on the platform. Don't go up.** He looked at it once, went to the brazier in the corner of the hall, and before Dongming's eyes threw it in. The paper curled once in the fire and was gone. He turned back and knelt: "None." Dongming didn't move; he only glanced at the skylight again.

That night a steward came into his room carrying a jade dish, and on it a pill; he didn't say what pill, only pried open Zhao Ang's mouth and put it in. He lay in pain all night, and at dawn he had built his foundation. Thirteen. He sat up, and the first thing he did was feel inside the scabbard. Empty. It had been the only letter anyone had ever written him.

Xiaoman lay on his bunk and by the moonlight at the window wrote his first letter home. The first line he wrote was "Ma, I've become an immortal" — rubbed out; the second, "Ma, I beat Ma Xiaobao" — he thought, if that got back to the village Ma San might come round, and rubbed it out too. In the end it came to these few lines:

**Ma: I've entered the immortals' gate. Five taels a year; the temple says it'll reach home in the twelfth month. Fix the roof. The basins can be put away — all seventeen. Buy Pa a pair of kneepads, dog-skin. Send Granny Wu another leg of venison — bought, this time. I'm fine here. When people bully me, I keep accounts. A few are paid already. — Xiaoman**

He folded it, thought, opened it again and added one line at the bottom: **Ma, a skimmer can carry water too.** He tucked the letter under his pillow; in the morning it would go to Zhou Heng and down the mountain on the same cart as the Shen family's five taels. Holding the token on his chest, he whispered: "That flatbread you owe me… still owed, right?" The token warmed, very lightly. As if to say: **Still owed.**
